doc.title: Jackie McLean — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
title: Sound, mouthpieces and his Selmer
summary: McLean says his tone is a mystery that stays the same whatever the reed, mouthpiece or horn; he has used a Selmer since 1965.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I want to – we can come there at a different point. Let’s talk about the idea of sound. There’s the instrument, there’s the setup piece, there’s the reed, there’s embouchure, there’s different – there’s ideas about timbre, and there’s the whole emotional component. Out of all those things, talk about how you rifled through all those things, consciously or unconsciously, in terms of what you think are the most important components of sound, of having a sound.

I think that what happens, when you put your mouth on the mouthpiece and blow into an instrument, is a mystery. It’s an enigma, because it’s something that’s structured in your face, your body, your wind that’s coming up through – from your lungs, that causes your instrument to sound a particular way. So I definitely didn’t like a

lot of sweet vibrato and sweet sound. So I worked real hard at getting a sound that was closer to the timbre of a tenor saxophone. Then, of course, trying to play more like Charlie Parker or Sonny Stitt, like that. But those were – I think that’s it. The rest of it is a mystery, because no matter what reed I put on or mouthpiece I put on, my tone always comes out the same. It comes out just like it always is.
Doesn’t make any difference. Doesn’t make a bit of difference.
I have – do you mean, my favorite saxophone?

I’m playing on a Selmer that I’ve been playing on for – since 1965. That’s a good instrument. I like – the Yamaha is a good instrument as well. But it just so happens that right now and for the last number of years I’ve been playing on the Selmer.
Is that an endorsement issue? Or that’s just what you’re playing?

It’s just what I’m playing on, yeah. And of course, they like for me to endorse their instrument. They’ll give me an instrument if I ask them for it. But I don’t want to keep getting instruments. I’ve got enough. I have – the instrument I’m playing on is fine. I just don’t want to have a room full of saxophones. I’d rather for them to give me money than saxophones.
